passage:
"Why are you angry?" Avni asked, passing the rotis.
Tejas looked up from his dal. "I'm not angry."
"Your face is angry."
"This is just my face."
"You haven't smiled since you came home."
"Because nothing funny happened. I'm eating."
Papa glanced over. "Avni, what makes you think he's upset?"
"His eyebrows are flat, and he isn't talking."
"He's chewing," Papa said. "Tejas, are you okay?"
"I'm fine. I'm thinking about the kite I'm making tomorrow."
Avni squinted. "So that was your kite face?"
"That was my normal face. This is my kite face." Tejas grinned hugely, and even Avni laughed.

qa.q: What was Tejas thinking about at dinner?
qa.a: The kite he was making tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Tejas actually feeling behind his flat face?
qa.a: He was calm and content, quietly planning his kite, not angry at all.

qa.q: How did Papa help clear up the misreading?
qa.a: He asked Avni what she was seeing, pointed out that Tejas was simply chewing, and then asked Tejas directly how he was 👍

qa.q: Why might Avni have read Tejas's face as angry?
qa.a: Avni saw flat eyebrows and silence and took them as anger, when he was just eating and thinking.

grounding: It shows a child's calm resting face being over-read as anger, and a parent checking rather than assuming.

passage:
Monday: During Hindi dictation, Disha crossed her eyes at Avni. Avni snorted so loudly that Ms Rao stopped reading, and Avni had to stand at the back, red-faced.
Wednesday: Disha did it again during silent reading. Avni pressed both lips together, stared hard at the book and dug a thumbnail into one palm. Avni's shoulders shook, but not a sound came out. When the bell rang, the two of them raced to the neem tree and laughed until they got hiccups.
Friday: In the class quiz Avni knew every answer and wanted to shout them all out, but sat on both hands and waited for a turn. Afterwards, Ms Rao let the whole class run two laps of the ground. Avni ran fastest of all.

qa.q: What did Disha do to make Avni laugh?
qa.a: Disha crossed her eyes at Avni.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling on Wednesday while the shoulders shook?
qa.a: Avni felt amused and bursting with laughter, but held it in with pressed lips and a thumbnail in the palm.

qa.q: What helped Avni's self-control work?
qa.a: Having ways to hold it in, like pressed lips and sitting on hands, and a release afterwards at the neem tree and on the laps.

qa.q: How might Ms Rao see the laps after the quiz?
qa.a: Ms Rao seems to know that children who have held themselves back need a chance to let the energy out, so the laps are a relief as much as a reward.

grounding: It illustrates a child growing the skill of holding in laughter and waiting for a turn, with chances to release energy afterwards.

passage:
Monday: It was Jaya's first day back at school after her fever. She walked home slowly, dragging her bag. When Noor from next door called, "Come and play langdi!", Jaya snapped, "Leave me alone!" and shut the door. Then she lay on the sofa with her shoes still on.
Tuesday: Amma cancelled Jaya's tuition for the week and let her skip chores. Jaya slept early. In the morning she knocked on Noor's door. "Sorry I shouted. I was so tired." Noor shrugged. "I thought you were cross with me."
Two weeks later: Jaya was still yawning through the afternoons and had stopped wanting to play at all. Amma watched her closely, then took her to the family doctor to check her sleep and whether anything else was wrong.

qa.q: What game did Noor call Jaya to play?
qa.a: Langdi.

qa.q: Why did Jaya snap at Noor on Monday?
qa.a: Jaya felt drained and exhausted after the fever, with nothing left for play, so the invitation felt like too much.

qa.q: What did Amma do as Jaya's tiredness went on?
qa.a: First she gave rest and fewer demands; when the weariness lasted and Jaya stopped wanting to play, she took her to the doctor to check sleep and health.

qa.q: How did Noor read Jaya's snapping?
qa.a: Noor thought Jaya was cross with her, not that Jaya was simply worn out.

grounding: It shows a school-age child drained after illness, moving slowly and snapping, needing rest and low demands, and a check-up when the exhaustion lasts.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: I'm Lokesh, and last month I was meant to read the thought for the day in assembly. We had been standing in the sun for ages. When I walked to the mike, my ears started buzzing and the ground felt tilted. Sangeeta, who was next in line, whispered, "You've gone white! Are you that scared?" I didn't know. Maybe I was scared. Maybe it was the sun, or that I had skipped breakfast. Mr Menon saw my face and didn't wait to find out. He sat me down on the steps in the shade, gave me water and sent Sangeeta running for the school nurse. The nurse checked me and called home. Sangeeta read the thought for the day instead. I read it the next week.

qa.q: What was Lokesh meant to read in assembly?
qa.a: The thought for the day.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when Sangeeta asked about being scared?
qa.a: Lokesh felt dizzy and confused, and honestly unsure whether the paleness came from fear, the sun or a skipped breakfast.

qa.q: Why was Mr Menon right not to wait to find out the cause?
qa.a: Sudden paleness with buzzing ears and a tilting feeling needs sitting down, water and adult help whatever the cause, so he acted and sent for the nurse.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta read Lokesh's white face?
qa.a: Sangeeta took it as stage fright, one possible reading, when heat or hunger might have caused it too.

grounding: It illustrates that a child going pale may be scared, overheated or unwell, and that paleness with dizziness calls for sitting down, water and adult help.

passage:
Saturday: Rekha came in from kho-kho with her fringe stuck to her forehead and sweat running down her neck. Her mother, Urmila, handed her water and laughed. "Who won?" "We did!"
Monday: Before the maths test, Rekha's palms were so damp that her pencil slipped. The fan was on and she hadn't run anywhere. She wiped her hands on her skirt and took a slow breath.
Thursday night: Rekha woke with her nightdress soaked, though the room was cool. She was shivering and her head ached. Urmila felt her forehead, sat with her, and in the morning took her to the doctor. On the way, Rekha said, "Three kinds of sweaty in one week." Urmila smiled. "And each one meant something different."

qa.q: What game had Rekha been playing on Saturday?
qa.a: Kho-kho.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling before the maths test when her palms were damp?
qa.a: She was nervous about the test; the fan was on and she hadn't been running, so the sweat most likely came from worry.

qa.q: What can help someone work out why a child is sweating?
qa.a: Looking at the setting and other signs, such as heat, a game, an upcoming test, or shivering and a headache, and getting a doctor's check when illness seems likely.

qa.q: How might Urmila have read Thursday night's sweat differently from Saturday's?
qa.a: On Saturday she saw a happy, hot child after a game; on Thursday the cool room, shivering and headache told her it was probably illness.

grounding: It shows the same sign, sweating, coming from exercise, test nerves and illness, with the setting and other signs telling them apart.

passage: At her Nana's tea stall beside the Rampur bus stand, Pooja poured a glass for Akash Bhaiya, the bus conductor. He took a sip and said, "Arre, this chai could wake the dead!" Pooja's face fell. Was it too strong? She nearly tipped it away. Instead she asked, "What do you mean, Bhaiya? Is it bad?" Akash laughed. "Bad? It's the best on my whole route. It means it's so strong it would wake anyone." Pooja grinned. Later, Nana looked at the darkening sky and said, "Hmm, the buses are getting fewer." Pooja thought about it, then asked, "Is that a hint that we're closing?" Nana chuckled and handed her the shutter hook.

qa.q: What did Akash say the chai could do?
qa.a: Wake the dead.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when her face fell?
qa.a: She felt worried and disappointed, thinking Akash meant the chai was too strong or bad.

qa.q: What habit helped Pooja understand both sayings?
qa.a: Asking what someone means instead of guessing, which saved good chai and helped her catch Nana's hint.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Pooja asked what he meant?
qa.a: Akash seemed amused and happy to explain, since he meant it as praise, not a complaint.

grounding: It illustrates a child meeting an idiom and a hint, and asking what someone meant instead of taking the words literally.

passage:
"Okay, Seema, one more! Say cheese!" Vaibhav bhaiya held up his phone.
"Cheeeese." Seema flashed a huge smile beside the mehendi stage.
"Perfect. Now go and sit, you've been dancing all day."
Later, scrolling, Vaibhav laughed. "Look at these two."
In the first, Seema was all teeth, eyes bright. In the second, taken a minute later, she was slumped on a plastic chair, eyelids half shut, a mehendi cone drooping in her hand.
"Delete that one!" Seema squealed. "I look sad."
"Were you sad?"
"No... just tired. My feet hurt from dancing."
"And in the smiling one, were you happy?"
Seema thought. "Kind of. Mostly I smiled because you said cheese."
"So both are true," said Vaibhav. "I'm keeping both."

qa.q: Where was Seema standing for the posed photo?
qa.a: Beside the mehendi stage.

qa.q: What was Seema really feeling in the candid photo?
qa.a: She was tired rather than sad, worn out with sore feet after dancing all day.

qa.q: Why is it worth keeping both kinds of photo?
qa.a: The posed smile shows Seema joining in, not necessarily her feeling, while the candid shot catches the real moment; together they tell a fuller story.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see the two photos?
qa.a: Vaibhav sees both as true: one shows Seema cooperating for the camera, the other shows how tired she really was.

grounding: It shows a child's posed 'cheese' smile as cooperation and a candid photo revealing tiredness, with each image telling a different story.

passage:
Monday: Manjula noticed a tiny line between Amma's eyebrows as she read something on her phone. Manjula's stomach dropped. Was it about the broken glass? Manjula went and asked, "Amma, are you upset with me?" Binita looked up, surprised. "No, kanna. Just an office email. Thank you for asking."
Wednesday: Amma's voice was lower than usual when she called everyone for dinner. Manjula watched her carefully, then checked: "Tired voice or cross voice?" Amma laughed hoarsely. "Sore-throat voice."
Saturday: Amma was quiet while packing for the trip to Nani's, a faint frown on her face. This time Manjula didn't guess. "Want help?" Amma handed over the folded towels and pressed her cheek to the top of Manjula's head.

qa.q: What did Amma call her lower voice on Wednesday?
qa.a: A sore-throat voice.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling on seeing the tiny line between Amma's eyebrows?
qa.a: Manjula felt worried and a little guilty, fearing Amma was upset about the broken glass.

qa.q: What stopped Manjula from over-reading the small cues?
qa.a: A short, direct check each time, asking instead of guessing, which kept each reading honest.

qa.q: How might Binita feel when Manjula keeps checking?
qa.a: Binita seems touched and grateful, thanking Manjula for asking and later pressing her cheek to Manjula's head.

grounding: It illustrates a child noticing a parent's slight frown and lower voice, and using a short check to avoid missing or over-reading subtle cues.

passage: The list on the notice board said: KIRAN J. – DRUMS, SCHOOL BAND. Kiran read it twice, and his face stayed perfectly still. Rohit, who hadn't been picked, was standing right beside him. On the bus Kiran stared out of the window, jaw tight, fingers tapping a secret rhythm on his knee. At the door of their flat in Kolkata, his mother, Aparna, took one look at him. "Such a serious face. Bad day?" "Normal day," Kiran said flatly. Aparna raised an eyebrow, noticed the tapping fingers, then folded her arms, smiling, and waited. Kiran lasted three more seconds. Then he dropped his bag. "I GOT DRUMS!" Aparna laughed. "I knew it. Your fingers told me."

qa.q: Which instrument was Kiran picked for?
qa.a: Drums, in the school band.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling behind his still face on the bus?
qa.a: He was thrilled and excited, as his fingers tapping a secret rhythm show, but kept a straight face, perhaps to spare Rohit or avoid teasing 🎉

qa.q: When can keeping a straight face at good news be kind?
qa.a: When someone close by, like Rohit, has just missed out, saving the celebration for later can spare their feelings.

qa.q: How did Aparna experience Kiran's serious face at the door?
qa.a: She saw through it thanks to the tapping fingers and clearly enjoyed waiting for him to burst.

grounding: It shows a child keeping a straight face while excited, waiting for the right moment, and a parent enjoying the delay.

passage: I'm Indu, and I was in the playground when the PE teacher announced that only Class 7 could use the new football at lunch. Vaibhav had been waiting all week for that ball. He said, "Okay, Sir," but his lips were pressed thin and his ears had gone red. He didn't argue. I can't be sure what he was thinking, but he walked off very stiffly. Behind the canteen he kicked the old ball against the wall, hard, again and again, until he was out of breath. Then he sat down next to me and said, "It's not fair. We're good players too." I said maybe he could ask Sir about taking turns. The next day he did, politely, and Sir agreed to Class 6 on Fridays.

qa.q: Which class could use the new football at lunch?
qa.a: Only Class 7.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav's thin lips and red ears suggest?
qa.a: He was probably angry and disappointed at a rule that felt unfair, even while staying polite, though Indu can't be sure.

qa.q: What gave Vaibhav's anger a safe outlet?
qa.a: Kicking the old ball against the wall behind the canteen, talking it over with Indu, and the next day raising the fairness politely.

qa.q: How might the PE teacher have seen Vaibhav's "Okay, Sir"?
qa.a: The teacher might have thought Vaibhav accepted the rule calmly, missing the anger underneath until the polite request the next day.

grounding: It illustrates a school-age child saying okay through tight lips at an unfair rule, and the anger finding a safe outlet afterwards, seen by a classmate.
